questions.stem: Which element produced the photoelectron spectrum shown?
questions.explanation: The peaks correspond to \(\mathrm{1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1}\): two, two, six, and one electrons. That is 11 electrons, so the element is sodium. Neon lacks the 3s peak, and magnesium would have a 3s peak of height 2.

questions.stem: Why is the peak at \(3.67\text{ MJ/mol}\) three times as tall as the peak at \(6.84\text{ MJ/mol}\)?
choices: The 2p electrons are three times as far from the nucleus.
The 2p electrons experience three times the nuclear charge.
The 2p subshell is filled before the 2s subshell.
It represents six 2p electrons, while the other peak represents two 2s electrons.
questions.explanation: Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons with that binding energy. The 2p subshell holds six electrons and the 2s subshell two.

questions.stem: The spectrum of magnesium is compared with the spectrum shown. Which describes how it differs?
choices: Every peak is at a lower binding energy, and the lowest-energy peak is twice as tall.
Every peak is at a higher binding energy, and the lowest-energy peak is twice as tall.
The peaks are at the same binding energies, but there is an additional peak.
Only the lowest-energy peak changes, shifting to a lower binding energy.
questions.explanation: Magnesium has one more proton, so every electron feels a greater attraction to the nucleus and has a higher binding energy. Its 3s subshell holds two electrons instead of one.

questions.stem: What is the average atomic mass of element X?
questions.explanation: The weighted average is \(24(0.79)+25(0.10)+26(0.11)=18.96+2.50+2.86=24.32\). The unweighted mean of the three masses is \(25.00\).

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the average atomic mass of element X is not a whole number?
choices: Protons and neutrons have masses that are not whole numbers.
Some atoms of X have lost electrons in the mass spectrometer.
Atoms of X have different numbers of protons.
The element exists as a mixture of isotopes with different numbers of neutrons, and the average is weighted by abundance.
questions.explanation: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons. Isotopes differ in neutrons, so a sample's average mass falls between the isotope masses, closest to the most abundant one.

figure.alt: Table of the successive ionization energies of element Z: first 578, second 1,817, third 2,745, and fourth 11,577 kilojoules per mole

questions.stem: Based on the successive ionization energies in the table, element Z is most likely in which group of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: The large jump occurs between the third and fourth ionization energies. Z has three valence electrons, and the fourth electron must come from a filled inner shell, much closer to the nucleus. Element Z is aluminum.

figure.alt: Table of the successive ionization energies of element Z: first 578, second 1,817, third 2,745, and fourth 11,577 kilojoules per mole

questions.stem: Based on the table, what is the most likely formula of the compound formed between element Z and oxygen?
questions.explanation: Z loses three electrons to form \(\mathrm{Z^{3+}}\), and oxygen gains two to form \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\). Two \(\mathrm{Z^{3+}}\) ions balance three \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) ions.

questions.stem: The first ionization energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen, even though oxygen has a greater nuclear charge. Which best explains this?
choices: Oxygen's valence electrons are in a higher energy level than nitrogen's.
Oxygen has a larger atomic radius than nitrogen.
Nitrogen's electron is removed from a 2s orbital.
In oxygen, the electron removed is paired in a 2p orbital, and repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen's three 2p electrons are each alone in an orbital. Oxygen's fourth 2p electron shares an orbital, and the added electron–electron repulsion slightly outweighs the increased nuclear charge.

questions.stem: Which of the following species has the largest radius: \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\), \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\), or \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\)?
questions.explanation: All four are isoelectronic, with 18 electrons. \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\) has the fewest protons, 16, so its electrons are held least tightly and it is largest.

questions.stem: What is the ground-state electron configuration of \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\)?
questions.explanation: Iron is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,4s^2\,3d^6}\). Transition metals lose their 4s electrons before their 3d electrons, so removing three electrons leaves \(\mathrm{3d^5}\).

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of nitrogen in ammonium sulfate, \(\mathrm{(NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}}\) (molar mass \(132.14\text{ g/mol}\))?
questions.explanation: Each formula unit contains two nitrogen atoms: \(\dfrac{2(14.01)}{132.14}\approx 21.2\%\). Counting only one nitrogen gives \(10.6\%\).

questions.stem: A compound is \(40.0\%\) carbon, \(6.7\%\) hydrogen, and \(53.3\%\) oxygen by mass, and its molar mass is \(180\text{ g/mol}\). What is its molecular formula?
questions.explanation: In \(100\text{ g}\): \(3.33\text{ mol C}\), \(6.6\text{ mol H}\), and \(3.33\text{ mol O}\), a ratio of 1:2:1, so the empirical formula is \(\mathrm{CH_{2}O}\) (\(30\text{ g/mol}\)). Since \(\tfrac{180}{30}=6\), the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}}\).

questions.stem: How many oxygen atoms are in \(4.40\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\)?
questions.explanation: \(4.40\text{ g}\) is \(0.100\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), which contains \(0.200\text{ mol}\) of O atoms, or \(0.200(6.02\times 10^{23})=1.20\times 10^{23}\) atoms.

questions.stem: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces \(0.880\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and \(0.360\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\). What is the empirical formula of the hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: Moles of C equal moles of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\): \(\tfrac{0.880}{44.01}=0.0200\). Moles of H are twice the moles of water: \(2\left(\tfrac{0.360}{18.02}\right)=0.0400\). The ratio is 1:2.

questions.stem: A \(1.00\text{ g}\) sample of impure calcium carbonate is heated, and all of the \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) decomposes: \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)\,\longrightarrow\,CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)}\). The sample loses \(0.396\text{ g}\) as \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), and the impurities do not react. What is the mass percent of \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) in the sample?
Which atom has the greatest second ionization energy: Na, Mg, Al, or Si?
questions.explanation: The second electron removed from sodium comes from the filled \(n=2\) shell, much closer to the nucleus and poorly shielded. The others lose a second valence electron.

questions.stem: Selenium is in the same group as sulfur. What is the formula of the compound formed between aluminum and selenium?
questions.explanation: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so selenium forms \(\mathrm{Se^{2-}}\) like \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\). With \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\), charge balance requires \(\mathrm{Al_{2}Se_{3}}\), matching \(\mathrm{Al_{2}S_{3}}\).

questions.stem: How many unpaired electrons are in a ground-state \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ion?
questions.explanation: Manganese is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,4s^2\,3d^5}\); losing the two 4s electrons leaves \(\mathrm{3d^5}\). By Hund's rule, each of the five d orbitals holds one electron.

questions.stem: How many neutrons and electrons are in \(^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\)?
questions.explanation: Neutrons equal the mass number minus the atomic number, \(56-26=30\). The 3+ charge means three fewer electrons than protons.

questions.stem: Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms?
questions.explanation: \(18.0\text{ g}\) of water is \(1.00\text{ mol}\) of molecules and \(3.00\text{ mol}\) of atoms. The others contain \(1.0\), \(2.00\), and \(1.0\text{ mol}\) of atoms.

questions.stem: In a photoelectron spectrum, the 1s peak of oxygen appears at a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of nitrogen. Which best explains this?
choices: Oxygen's 1s electrons are farther from the nucleus.
Oxygen has more 1s electrons than nitrogen.
Oxygen has more protons, so its 1s electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus.
Oxygen's valence electrons shield the 1s electrons from the nucleus.
questions.explanation: Both 1s subshells hold two electrons at nearly the same distance, with essentially no shielding. The greater nuclear charge of oxygen increases the Coulombic attraction.

questions.stem: What mass of magnesium contains the same number of atoms as \(12.0\text{ g}\) of carbon?
questions.explanation: \(12.0\text{ g}\) of carbon is \(1.00\text{ mol}\). The same number of magnesium atoms, \(1.00\text{ mol}\), has a mass equal to the molar mass of Mg, \(24.3\text{ g}\).

figure.alt: Potential energy versus internuclear distance for two diatomic molecules. Curve A has a deep minimum of −436 kJ/mol at 74 pm. Curve B has a shallower minimum of −242 kJ/mol at 199 pm. Both curves rise steeply at short distances and level off toward zero at long distances

questions.stem: Which statement about the molecules represented by curves A and B is correct?
choices: A has the stronger and shorter bond.
B has the stronger and shorter bond.
A has the stronger but longer bond.
B has the stronger but shorter bond.
questions.explanation: The depth of each minimum is the bond energy, and its position is the bond length. Curve A's minimum is deeper, \(-436\text{ kJ/mol}\), and occurs at a shorter distance, 74 pm.

figure.alt: Potential energy versus internuclear distance for two diatomic molecules. Curve A has a deep minimum of −436 kJ/mol at 74 pm. Curve B has a shallower minimum of −242 kJ/mol at 199 pm. Both curves rise steeply at short distances and level off toward zero at long distances

questions.stem: Why does the potential energy rise steeply at very short internuclear distances on both curves?
choices: The electrons are no longer attracted to either nucleus.
The bond breaks and the atoms separate.
The positively charged nuclei repel each other strongly when they are forced close together.
questions.explanation: At distances shorter than the bond length, nucleus–nucleus and electron–electron repulsions dominate the attractions, so energy rises sharply.

figure.alt: Potential energy versus internuclear distance for two diatomic molecules. Curve A has a deep minimum of −436 kJ/mol at 74 pm. Curve B has a shallower minimum of −242 kJ/mol at 199 pm. Both curves rise steeply at short distances and level off toward zero at long distances

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to break one mole of the bonds represented by curve B, separating the atoms completely?
questions.explanation: Separating the atoms raises the energy from the minimum, \(-242\text{ kJ/mol}\), to \(0\) at large distances. The value 199 is the bond length in picometers.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greatest lattice energy: NaF, NaCl, KBr, or MgO?
questions.explanation: Coulombic attraction is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely related to the distance between ions. MgO has charges of \(2+\) and \(2-\), quadrupling the product, and its ions are small.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride melts at \(801^\circ\text{C}\), and cesium iodide melts at \(632^\circ\text{C}\). Which best explains the difference?
choices: NaCl has a greater difference in electronegativity.
\(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) are smaller than \(\mathrm{Cs^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\), so they are closer together and attract each other more strongly.
CsI contains covalent bonds that break more easily.
questions.explanation: The charges are the same in both compounds, so the difference comes from ionic radius. Smaller ions sit closer together, giving stronger Coulombic attraction and a higher melting point.

questions.stem: Steel is made by adding small amounts of carbon to iron. Which diagram better represents steel, and how does the carbon change the metal?
choices: Y; the carbon atoms replace iron atoms, making the alloy softer.
X; the carbon atoms fill spaces in the lattice, making the alloy harder and less malleable than iron.
X; the carbon atoms make the alloy more malleable by spreading the iron atoms apart.
Y; carbon atoms are similar in size to iron atoms.
questions.explanation: Carbon atoms are much smaller than iron atoms and occupy interstitial spaces. They interfere with layers of iron atoms sliding past one another, which makes steel harder and less malleable.

questions.stem: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Which diagram better represents brass, and why?
choices: X, because zinc atoms are much smaller than copper atoms.
Y, because zinc forms ionic bonds with copper.
X, because zinc atoms fill the spaces between copper atoms.
Y, because copper and zinc atoms have similar radii, so zinc atoms can replace copper atoms in the lattice.
questions.explanation: Substitutional alloys form when the atoms of the two metals are close in size, as copper and zinc are. Atoms of one element take the places of atoms of the other.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why metals conduct electricity in the solid state?
choices: Their valence electrons are delocalized and free to move throughout the lattice of metal cations.
Their ions are free to move through the solid.
They contain no electrons in their outer shells.
Their atoms are held together by strong covalent bonds.
questions.explanation: In the electron-sea model, valence electrons are shared among all of the cations and move freely, carrying current. Ionic solids conduct only when melted or dissolved, when their ions can move.

questions.stem: A solid has a high melting point, is brittle, and does not conduct electricity, but it conducts when melted. Which type of solid is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Ionic solids have strong Coulombic attractions, so they melt at high temperatures and shatter when layers shift and like charges meet. Their ions conduct only when free to move.

questions.stem: What is the molecular geometry of \(\mathrm{SF_{4}}\)?
questions.explanation: Sulfur has four bonding pairs and one lone pair, five electron domains in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, giving a seesaw shape.

questions.stem: What are the molecular geometry and polarity of \(\mathrm{XeF_{4}}\)?
questions.explanation: Xenon has four bonding pairs and two lone pairs. The lone pairs sit opposite each other in an octahedral arrangement, leaving a square planar shape in which the bond dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: Which molecule is polar?
questions.explanation: \(\mathrm{NF_{3}}\) is trigonal pyramidal because of the lone pair on nitrogen, so its bond dipoles do not cancel. The other molecules are symmetric, and their bond dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: Which lists \(\mathrm{CH_{4}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\), and \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) in order of decreasing H–X–H bond angle?
questions.explanation: All three have four electron domains. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angles: about \(109.5^\circ\), \(107^\circ\), and \(104.5^\circ\).

questions.stem: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in HCN and of the carbon atom in formaldehyde, \(\mathrm{H_{2}CO}\)?
choices: sp2 in HCN and sp3 in \(\mathrm{H_{2}CO}\)
sp in HCN and sp2 in \(\mathrm{H_{2}CO}\)
questions.explanation: Carbon in HCN has two electron domains, a single bond and a triple bond, so it is sp. Carbon in formaldehyde has three domains, two single bonds and a double bond, so it is sp2.

questions.stem: How many sigma bonds and pi bonds are in acrylonitrile, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}C{\equiv}N}\)?
questions.explanation: There are three C–H bonds, the C=C double bond, the C–C single bond, and the triple bond. Each bond contains one sigma bond, for a total of 6. The double bond adds one pi bond and the triple bond two.

questions.stem: In the Lewis structure of the nitrate ion, \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\), what is the formal charge on the nitrogen atom?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has four bonds, from one double and two single bonds, and no lone pairs: \(5-0-\tfrac{8}{2}=+1\). The single-bonded oxygen atoms each carry \(-1\), giving the ion's overall \(-1\) charge.

questions.stem: In the carbonate ion, \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}\), how do the three carbon–oxygen bonds compare?
choices: One is shorter than the other two.
All three have the same length, between that of a single and a double bond.
They alternate between single and double bonds over time.
questions.explanation: Carbonate has three resonance structures. The actual ion is a single hybrid in which each bond has a bond order of \(\tfrac{4}{3}\), so all three bonds are identical.

questions.stem: Which lists the carbon–oxygen bond length in CO, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), and \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}\) from shortest to longest?
questions.explanation: Bond orders are 3 in CO, 2 in \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), and \(\tfrac{4}{3}\) in carbonate. Higher bond order means more shared electrons and a shorter bond.

questions.stem: \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}}\) exists, but \(\mathrm{NCl_{5}}\) does not. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Nitrogen has fewer valence electrons than phosphorus.
Nitrogen is more electronegative than chlorine.
Phosphorus has a smaller atomic radius than nitrogen.
Nitrogen is in the second period and is too small to accommodate more than four electron domains around it.
questions.explanation: Atoms from the third period and beyond, such as phosphorus, can be surrounded by more than eight electrons. Second-period atoms are limited to an octet.

questions.stem: Silicon dioxide melts above \(1600^\circ\text{C}\), while carbon dioxide sublimes at \(-78^\circ\text{C}\). Which best explains the difference?
choices: \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\) is a network covalent solid held together by covalent bonds throughout, while \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) molecules are held together only by weak London dispersion forces.
\(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) contains double bonds, which are weaker than single bonds.
Silicon is less electronegative than carbon.
questions.explanation: Melting \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\) requires breaking strong covalent bonds, while subliming \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) only overcomes intermolecular forces between nonpolar molecules.

questions.stem: Which statement about \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) is correct?
choices: Both are nonpolar because both are tetrahedral.
Both are polar because C–Cl bonds are polar.
\(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\) is polar and \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) is nonpolar, although both are tetrahedral.
questions.explanation: In \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\), four identical bond dipoles cancel. In \(\mathrm{CH_{2}Cl_{2}}\), the C–Cl and C–H dipoles differ, so the molecule has a net dipole.

questions.stem: Which species has an odd number of valence electrons and therefore cannot have every atom with a complete octet?
questions.explanation: \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) has \(5+2(6)=17\) valence electrons. With an odd number, at least one atom must have an unpaired electron.

questions.stem: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the central xenon atom in the Lewis structure of \(\mathrm{XeF_{2}}\)?
questions.explanation: Xenon contributes 8 valence electrons. Two are used in the bonds to fluorine, leaving 6 as three lone pairs. The five domains form a trigonal bipyramid with the lone pairs equatorial, so the molecule is linear.

questions.stem: Which liquid shown has the strongest intermolecular forces?
choices: All three are equal at their boiling points.
questions.explanation: Stronger intermolecular forces lower the vapor pressure at any temperature and raise the boiling point. Liquid C has the lowest vapor pressure and the highest normal boiling point, \(100^\circ\text{C}\).

questions.stem: According to the graph, at about what temperature does liquid B boil when the external pressure is \(50\text{ kPa}\)?
questions.explanation: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure. Curve B reaches \(50\text{ kPa}\) near \(60^\circ\text{C}\); at lower external pressure, the boiling point is lower.

questions.stem: At \(25^\circ\text{C}\), which liquid shown evaporates most readily, and why?
choices: C, because its molecules have the most kinetic energy
B, because it has an intermediate boiling point
A, because its molecules are held by the weakest intermolecular forces, so more of them can escape the liquid
All evaporate equally, because they are at the same temperature
questions.explanation: At the same temperature, molecules of all three liquids have the same average kinetic energy. The fraction with enough energy to overcome the attractions is largest for the liquid with the weakest attractions.

questions.stem: The graph shows speed distributions for helium and nitrogen at the same temperature. Which gas is represented by curve Y, and why?
choices: Helium, because at the same temperature lighter molecules have higher speeds
Nitrogen, because heavier molecules move faster
Helium, because helium has a higher average kinetic energy
Nitrogen, because its curve is broader
questions.explanation: At the same temperature, both gases have the same average kinetic energy, \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Helium's much smaller mass gives it higher speeds and a broader distribution.

questions.stem: A gas has a density of \(1.25\text{ g/L}\) at \(273\text{ K}\) and \(1.00\text{ atm}\). Which gas could it be? Use \(R=0.08206\text{ L}\cdot\text{atm/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}\).
questions.explanation: \(M=\dfrac{dRT}{P}=\dfrac{(1.25)(0.08206)(273)}{1.00}\approx 28.0\text{ g/mol}\), the molar mass of \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\).

questions.explanation: The mole fraction of X is \(\tfrac{6}{10}=0.60\), so \(P_X=0.60(2.0)=1.2\text{ atm}\). The larger size of the Y particles does not affect partial pressure in an ideal gas.

questions.stem: Under which conditions does a sample of ammonia deviate most from ideal gas behavior?
questions.explanation: At high pressure the volume of the molecules themselves becomes significant, and at low temperature the attractions between molecules, including hydrogen bonds in ammonia, have a larger effect.

questions.stem: At the same temperature, how does the average speed of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) molecules compare with the average speed of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) molecules?
questions.explanation: Average speed is proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\). The ratio is \(\sqrt{\tfrac{32}{2}}=4\).

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving \(5.85\text{ g}\) of NaCl in enough water to make \(250.0\text{ mL}\) of solution?
A student dilutes \(25.0\text{ mL}\) of \(6.0\text{ M}\) HCl to a total volume of \(150.0\text{ mL}\). What is the concentration of the diluted solution?
questions.explanation: Moles are conserved: \(M_2=\dfrac{(6.0)(25.0)}{150.0}=1.0\text{ M}\). Adding \(150\text{ mL}\) of water, rather than diluting to \(150\text{ mL}\) total, would give about \(0.86\text{ M}\).

questions.stem: A student's cuvette has fingerprints on it when the unknown solution is measured, but not when the calibration standards were measured. How does this affect the calculated concentration?
choices: It is too low, because fingerprints reduce absorbance.
It is unaffected, because concentration does not depend on the cuvette.
It is too high, because the fingerprints absorb or scatter light and increase the measured absorbance.
It is unaffected, because the calibration line passes through the origin.
questions.explanation: The spectrophotometer attributes all lost light to the solution. A falsely high absorbance, read on the calibration line, gives a falsely high concentration.

questions.stem: The paper is polar, and the solvent is nonpolar. Which conclusion about components A and B is supported by the chromatogram?
choices: A is more polar than B, because it is attracted more strongly to the polar paper and moves less.
B is more polar than A, because it travels farther.
A has a greater molar mass than B.
A and B have the same polarity, because they started together.
questions.explanation: Components that interact strongly with the stationary phase move slowly. Polar A is held by the polar paper, while less polar B dissolves well in the nonpolar solvent and travels farther.

questions.stem: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane both have the formula \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}}\). Pentane boils at \(36^\circ\text{C}\), and 2,2-dimethylpropane boils at \(10^\circ\text{C}\). Which best explains this?
choices: Pentane forms hydrogen bonds, and 2,2-dimethylpropane does not.
The straight-chain shape of pentane allows greater surface contact, producing stronger London dispersion forces.
questions.explanation: The molecules have the same number of electrons and are both nonpolar. Compact, branched molecules have less surface area for dispersion attractions than long chains.

questions.stem: Acetone, \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{2}CO}\), mixes completely with water. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The oxygen atom of acetone can accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules.
Acetone molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other.
Acetone is ionic and dissociates in water.
questions.explanation: Acetone has no H bonded to N, O, or F, so it cannot hydrogen-bond with itself. Its polar carbonyl oxygen, however, can accept hydrogen bonds from water.

questions.stem: Iodine, \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\), dissolves much more readily in carbon tetrachloride than in water. Which best explains this?
choices: Water is nonpolar, and \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) is polar.
Both \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) are nonpolar, so the dispersion forces between them are similar to those within each pure substance.
questions.explanation: Dissolving iodine in water would require breaking water's strong hydrogen bonds and replacing them with weaker attractions. Iodine and \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) have comparable attractions, so mixing is favorable.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of light with a wavelength of \(500\text{ nm}\)? Use \(h=6.626\times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\) and \(c=3.00\times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
questions.explanation: \(E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{(6.626\times 10^{-34})(3.00\times 10^8)}{500\times 10^{-9}}=3.98\times 10^{-19}\text{ J}\). Forgetting to convert nanometers to meters gives \(3.98\times 10^{-28}\).

questions.stem: Which type of electromagnetic radiation is most likely to cause electronic transitions in molecules?
questions.explanation: UV and visible photons have energies matching electronic transitions. Infrared radiation excites molecular vibrations, and microwaves excite rotations.

questions.stem: Water, \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\), boils at \(100^\circ\text{C}\), while hydrogen sulfide, \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\), boils at \(-60^\circ\text{C}\), although \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\) has more electrons. Which best explains this?
choices: Water has stronger covalent O–H bonds that must break when it boils.
Water has stronger London dispersion forces.
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are much stronger than the dipole–dipole and dispersion forces in \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\).
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules without breaking covalent bonds. Hydrogen bonding, possible because oxygen is small and highly electronegative, outweighs the larger dispersion forces of \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\).

questions.stem: A \(2.00\text{ L}\) flask at \(300\text{ K}\) contains \(0.100\text{ mol}\) of He and \(0.200\text{ mol}\) of Ne. What is the total pressure? Use \(R=0.08206\text{ L}\cdot\text{atm/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}\).
questions.explanation: Total pressure depends only on the total moles of gas: \(P=\dfrac{(0.300)(0.08206)(300)}{2.00}=3.69\text{ atm}\). The value \(2.46\text{ atm}\) is the partial pressure of Ne.

questions.stem: Which compound has the highest boiling point: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{3}}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}F}\), or \(\mathrm{CH_{3}Cl}\)?
questions.explanation: Methanol has an H atom bonded to O, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another. In \(\mathrm{CH_{3}F}\), fluorine is bonded to carbon, not hydrogen, so it cannot hydrogen-bond with itself.

questions.explanation: Only silver and chloride ions combine to form the insoluble product. Sodium and nitrate ions are spectator ions, and sodium nitrate is soluble.

questions.stem: Which is the net ionic equation for the reaction of acetic acid with sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Acetic acid is a weak acid, so it is mostly un-ionized and is written as a molecule. Only strong acids are written as \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\).

questions.stem: The reaction \(\mathrm{2H_{2}(g)\,+\,O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2H_{2}O(g)}\) goes to completion in the container shown. Which describes the contents afterward?
questions.explanation: Six \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) molecules need only three \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) molecules, so \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) is limiting. Six molecules of water form, and one of the four \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) molecules remains.

questions.stem: Aluminum reacts with oxygen: \(\mathrm{4Al(s)\,+\,3O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2Al_{2}O_{3}(s)}\). What mass of \(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}\) (molar mass \(101.96\text{ g/mol}\)) forms from \(10.0\text{ g}\) of Al with excess oxygen?
questions.explanation: \(\tfrac{10.0}{26.98}=0.371\text{ mol Al}\), which forms \(\tfrac{2}{4}(0.371)=0.185\text{ mol}\) \(\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}\), or \(18.9\text{ g}\). Ignoring the 2:4 ratio gives \(37.8\text{ g}\).

questions.stem: What mass of water can form when \(4.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) reacts with \(16.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(2.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) and \(0.50\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\). The hydrogen would need \(1.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\), so \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) is limiting and forms \(1.0\text{ mol}\), or \(18\text{ g}\), of water. Mass is conserved, but \(20\text{ g}\) includes unreacted hydrogen.

questions.stem: The theoretical yield of a reaction is \(18.0\text{ g}\), and \(15.3\text{ g}\) of product is recovered. What is the percent yield?
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{15.3}{18.0}\times 100=85.0\%\). A percent yield above \(100\%\) would suggest a wet or impure product.

questions.stem: A \(25.00\text{ mL}\) sample of HCl is titrated to the equivalence point with \(18.40\text{ mL}\) of \(0.100\text{ M}\) NaOH. What is the concentration of the HCl?
questions.explanation: \(\text{mol NaOH}=0.01840(0.100)=1.84\times 10^{-3}\), which equals the moles of HCl. Dividing by \(0.02500\text{ L}\) gives \(0.0736\text{ M}\).

questions.stem: A \(20.0\text{ mL}\) sample of \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\) is completely neutralized by \(30.0\text{ mL}\) of \(0.200\text{ M}\) NaOH. What is the concentration of the \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\)?
questions.explanation: \(6.00\times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) neutralizes \(3.00\times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\), which supplies two \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) per formula unit. Dividing by \(0.0200\text{ L}\) gives \(0.150\text{ M}\).

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion, \(\mathrm{Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-}}\)?
questions.explanation: Seven oxygen atoms contribute \(-14\). For a total of \(-2\), the two chromium atoms total \(+12\), so each is \(+6\).

questions.stem: In the reaction \(\mathrm{Zn(s)\,+\,Cu^{2+}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,Zn^{2+}(aq)\,+\,Cu(s)}\), which species is the oxidizing agent?
questions.explanation: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) gains electrons and is reduced, so it oxidizes zinc. The oxidizing agent is the species that is itself reduced.

questions.stem: When \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}(aq)\,+\,Fe^{2+}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,Mn^{2+}(aq)\,+\,Fe^{3+}(aq)}\) is balanced in acidic solution, what is the ratio of \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\)?
questions.explanation: Manganese changes from \(+7\) to \(+2\), gaining five electrons, while each iron loses one. Five \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ions supply the electrons for one \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\).

questions.stem: In acidic solution, \(15.0\text{ mL}\) of \(0.0200\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{KMnO_{4}}\) is needed to oxidize all of the \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) in a sample. How many moles of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) were in the sample?
questions.explanation: \(0.0150(0.0200)=3.00\times 10^{-4}\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{MnO_{4}^{-}}\), and each reacts with five \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), giving \(1.50\times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}\).

questions.stem: Which process is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance, iron oxide, by breaking and forming chemical bonds. The others change only the state or the arrangement of particles, overcoming intermolecular forces.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes: \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)\,\longrightarrow\,CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)}\). What volume of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) forms from \(10.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) at \(273\text{ K}\) and \(1.00\text{ atm}\)?
Which pair of aqueous solutions produces a precipitate when mixed?
questions.explanation: Lead(II) iodide, \(\mathrm{PbI_{2}}\), is insoluble. All sodium, potassium, ammonium, and nitrate salts are soluble, so the other mixtures contain only dissolved ions.

questions.stem: In the reaction \(\mathrm{HCO_{3}^{-}(aq)\,+\,H_{2}O(l)\,\rightleftharpoons\,CO_{3}^{2-}(aq)\,+\,H_{3}O^{+}(aq)}\), which species are the Brønsted–Lowry acids?
questions.explanation: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton. \(\mathrm{HCO_{3}^{-}}\) donates one in the forward direction, and \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\) donates one in the reverse direction.

questions.stem: All of the chloride in a sample is precipitated as AgCl (molar mass \(143.32\text{ g/mol}\)), giving \(0.287\text{ g}\) of precipitate. What mass of chloride was in the sample?
questions.explanation: \(\tfrac{0.287}{143.32}=0.00200\text{ mol}\) of AgCl, containing \(0.00200\text{ mol}\) of Cl, or \(0.00200(35.45)=0.0709\text{ g}\). The value \(0.216\text{ g}\) is the mass of silver.

questions.stem: Which statement about the energy changes in a chemical reaction is correct?
choices: Breaking bonds absorbs energy, and forming bonds releases energy.
Breaking bonds releases energy, and forming bonds absorbs energy.
Both breaking and forming bonds release energy.
Only exothermic reactions involve breaking bonds.
questions.explanation: Separating bonded atoms requires energy to overcome their attraction. A reaction is exothermic when more energy is released by forming bonds than is absorbed in breaking them.

questions.stem: A student writes the reaction of solid magnesium with hydrochloric acid as \(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,+\,2H^{+}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,+\,H_{2}(g)}\). Which statement about this equation is true?
choices: It is unbalanced, because the charges differ on the two sides.
It omits chloride ions, which take part in the reaction.
It is an acid–base reaction, not a redox reaction.
It is a balanced net ionic equation for a redox reaction, with charge and atoms conserved.
questions.explanation: Both sides have a charge of \(2+\) and the same atoms. Magnesium is oxidized from 0 to \(+2\), and hydrogen is reduced from \(+1\) to 0; chloride ions are spectators.

questions.stem: What mass of NaOH (molar mass \(40.00\text{ g/mol}\)) is needed to prepare \(250.0\text{ mL}\) of \(0.150\text{ M}\) solution?
questions.explanation: The solution requires \(0.2500(0.150)=0.0375\text{ mol}\), which is \(0.0375(40.00)=1.50\text{ g}\). Using \(1\text{ L}\) instead of \(0.250\text{ L}\) gives \(6.00\text{ g}\).

questions.stem: In a titration, a student fails to rinse the buret with the NaOH titrant, so the titrant is diluted by water left in the buret. How does this affect the calculated concentration of the acid?
choices: It is too low, because the titrant reacts with water.
It is too high, because more titrant volume is needed to reach the equivalence point.
It is unaffected, because the moles of acid do not change.
It is too low, because less titrant volume is needed.
questions.explanation: The diluted base delivers fewer moles per milliliter, so a larger volume is needed. The calculation multiplies that volume by the original, higher molarity, overestimating the moles of base and thus of acid.

questions.stem: What mass of ammonia can form from \(28.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) and \(9.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\), by \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g)\,+\,3H_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2NH_{3}(g)}\)?
questions.explanation: There are \(1.00\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) and \(4.46\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\). The nitrogen needs only \(3.00\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\), so \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) is limiting and forms \(2.00\text{ mol}\), or \(34.1\text{ g}\), of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\).

figure.alt: Initial-rate data for the reaction of A and B. Experiment 1: [A] 0.10 M, [B] 0.10 M, rate 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. Experiment 2: [A] 0.20 M, [B] 0.10 M, rate 8.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. Experiment 3: [A] 0.10 M, [B] 0.30 M, rate 6.0 × 10⁻³ M/s

questions.stem: Based on the data in the table, what is the rate law for the reaction?
questions.explanation: Doubling [A] (experiments 1 and 2) quadruples the rate, so the reaction is second order in A. Tripling [B] (experiments 1 and 3) triples the rate, so it is first order in B.

figure.alt: Initial-rate data for the reaction of A and B. Experiment 1: [A] 0.10 M, [B] 0.10 M, rate 2.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. Experiment 2: [A] 0.20 M, [B] 0.10 M, rate 8.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. Experiment 3: [A] 0.10 M, [B] 0.30 M, rate 6.0 × 10⁻³ M/s

questions.stem: Based on the data in the table, what is the rate constant, including units?
questions.explanation: From experiment 1: \(k=\dfrac{2.0\times 10^{-3}}{(0.10)^2(0.10)}=2.0\). For a third-order rate law, the units of \(k\) are \(\text{M}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}\), so that the rate has units of \(\text{M/s}\).

questions.stem: Using the rate law from the table, what is the initial rate when \([\mathrm{A}]_0=0.30\text{ M}\) and \([\mathrm{B}]_0=0.20\text{ M}\)?
questions.explanation: \(\text{rate}=2.0(0.30)^2(0.20)=0.036\text{ M/s}\). Tripling [A] multiplies the rate by 9 and doubling [B] multiplies it by 2, so the rate is 18 times the rate in experiment 1.

choices: Zero order, because the graph is a straight line
Second order, because the slope is negative
First order, because ln[X] decreases linearly with time
It cannot be determined from one graph.
questions.explanation: A plot of ln[X] versus time is linear only for a first-order reaction. Zero-order reactions give linear plots of [X] versus time, and second-order reactions give linear plots of \(\tfrac{1}{[X]}\) versus time.

questions.explanation: The slope is \(\dfrac{-3.0-(-1.0)}{400}=-0.0050\text{ s}^{-1}\), so \(k=0.0050\text{ s}^{-1}\). For a first-order reaction, \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{k}=\dfrac{0.693}{0.0050}\approx 139\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: For a second-order reaction with rate law \(\text{rate}=k[\mathrm{A}]^2\), which plot gives a straight line?
choices: \(\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]}\) versus time, with a slope of \(k\)
\(\ln[\mathrm{A}]\) versus time, with a slope of \(-k\)
\([\mathrm{A}]\) versus time, with a slope of \(-k\)
\([\mathrm{A}]^2\) versus time, with a slope of \(k\)
questions.explanation: The integrated rate law for second order is \(\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]}=kt+\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{A}]_0}\), a line with slope \(k\).

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of \(20\text{ min}\). What percentage of the reactant remains after \(1.0\text{ hour}\)?
questions.explanation: One hour is three half-lives, so \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^3=12.5\%\) remains. A first-order half-life does not depend on concentration.

figure.alt: Potential energy diagram for a two-step reaction. Reactants start at 0 kJ/mol. The first transition state, labeled 1, is at about 91 kJ/mol. An intermediate, I, sits in a valley at about 20 kJ/mol. The second transition state, labeled 2, is at about 46 kJ/mol. Products end at about −40 kJ/mol

questions.stem: Which step of the mechanism represented in the diagram is rate-determining, and what is I?
choices: Step 1, because it has the higher activation energy; I is a reaction intermediate.
Step 2, because it comes last; I is a catalyst.
Step 1, because it is exothermic; I is a transition state.
Step 2, because it has the higher activation energy; I is a product.
questions.explanation: The slow step has the largest energy barrier from its starting point: about \(91\text{ kJ/mol}\) for step 1 compared with about \(26\text{ kJ/mol}\) for step 2. I is formed in step 1 and used up in step 2.

figure.alt: Potential energy diagram for a two-step reaction. Reactants start at 0 kJ/mol. The first transition state, labeled 1, is at about 91 kJ/mol. An intermediate, I, sits in a valley at about 20 kJ/mol. The second transition state, labeled 2, is at about 46 kJ/mol. Products end at about −40 kJ/mol

questions.stem: According to the diagram, what are the activation energy of the forward reaction's first step and the overall enthalpy change of the reaction?
questions.explanation: Step 1 rises from the reactants at \(0\) to the first peak at about \(91\text{ kJ/mol}\). The products are about \(40\text{ kJ/mol}\) below the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.stem: Which effect does a catalyst have on a reaction?
choices: It lowers \(\Delta H\), making the reaction more exothermic.
It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, speeding up both the forward and reverse reactions without changing \(\Delta H\).
It shifts the equilibrium toward products.
It increases the kinetic energy of the reactant molecules.
questions.explanation: A catalyst changes the mechanism, not the starting or ending energies. Because both directions are sped up equally, the equilibrium constant is unchanged.

questions.stem: The reaction \(\mathrm{2NO(g)\,+\,O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2NO_{2}(g)}\) has the rate law \(\text{rate}=k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{O_2}]\). Which mechanism is consistent with this rate law?
questions.explanation: The slow step gives \(\text{rate}=k_2[\mathrm{N_2O_2}][\mathrm{O_2}]\). From the fast equilibrium, \([\mathrm{N_2O_2}]\) is proportional to \([\mathrm{NO}]^2\), so the rate law becomes \(k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{O_2}]\). The third mechanism's slow step would give \(k[\mathrm{NO}]^2\).

figure.alt: Distributions of collision energies for one reaction mixture at two temperatures, T1 and T2. The T1 curve is taller with a peak at lower energy. The T2 curve is lower, broader, and shifted to higher energies. A dashed vertical line marks the activation energy, far to the right; the area under the T2 curve beyond this line is much larger than under the T1 curve

questions.stem: Which statement best explains, using the diagram, why the reaction is much faster at \(T_2\) than at \(T_1\)?
choices: The activation energy is lower at \(T_2\).
The number of molecules is greater at \(T_2\).
Collisions at \(T_2\) are always correctly oriented.
A much larger fraction of collisions at \(T_2\) has energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
questions.explanation: Raising the temperature shifts the distribution to higher energies. Because the activation energy lies far out in the tail, a modest shift greatly increases the area beyond \(E_a\).

questions.stem: Two molecules collide with more than enough energy to react, but no reaction occurs. Which best explains this?
choices: The molecules were not oriented correctly when they collided.
The activation energy was too high.
questions.explanation: An effective collision requires both sufficient energy and the proper orientation, so that the atoms that form new bonds come into contact.

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{2N_{2}O_{5}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,4NO_{2}(g)\,+\,O_{2}(g)}\), \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{5}}\) is consumed at \(0.020\text{ M/s}\). At what rate is \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) produced?
questions.explanation: The coefficients show that four \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) form for every two \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{5}}\) consumed, so \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) forms twice as fast.

questions.stem: The elementary step \(\mathrm{NO_{2}\,+\,CO\,\longrightarrow\,NO\,+\,CO_{2}}\) occurs in a single collision. What is its rate law?
choices: It cannot be determined without experimental data.
questions.explanation: For an elementary step only, the rate law follows from the molecularity. A bimolecular collision between \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) and CO is first order in each.

questions.stem: The rate law for a reaction is \(\text{rate}=k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\). In an experiment, B is present at \(1000\) times the concentration of A. How will a plot of ln[A] versus time appear?
choices: Curved, because the reaction is second order overall
Linear, because the reaction is zero order in B
Linear, because [B] stays nearly constant and the reaction behaves as first order in A
Horizontal, because A reacts too slowly to measure
questions.explanation: With B in large excess, its concentration barely changes, so \(k[\mathrm{B}]\) is effectively a constant. The reaction is pseudo-first order in A.

questions.stem: What are the units of the rate constant for a zero-order reaction?
questions.explanation: For zero order, \(\text{rate}=k\), so \(k\) has the units of rate, \(\text{M/s}\). First-order constants have units of \(\text{s}^{-1}\).

questions.stem: Powdered zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid much faster than a single lump of zinc of the same mass. Which best explains this?
choices: The powder has more surface area, so more zinc atoms can collide with \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ions per second.
The powder has a lower activation energy.
The powder is at a higher temperature.
The powder contains more moles of zinc.
questions.explanation: Reactions of solids occur at the surface. Increasing surface area increases the frequency of collisions without changing the activation energy.

questions.stem: How does an increase in temperature affect the rate constant \(k\) of a reaction?
choices: \(k\) is unaffected, because it is a constant.
\(k\) increases, because more collisions have enough energy to overcome the activation energy.
\(k\) increases only if a catalyst is present.
questions.explanation: The rate constant depends on temperature through the fraction of energetic collisions. It is constant only at a given temperature.

questions.stem: For a first-order reaction with \(k=0.0231\text{ min}^{-1}\), what is the half-life?
A zero-order reaction has a rate constant of \(0.010\text{ M/s}\). If the initial concentration of reactant is \(0.50\text{ M}\), how long does it take for the reactant to be used up?
questions.explanation: For zero order, \([\mathrm{A}]=[\mathrm{A}]_0-kt\). Setting \([\mathrm{A}]=0\) gives \(t=\dfrac{0.50}{0.010}=50\text{ s}\). Its half-life, \(25\text{ s}\), is not constant.

questions.stem: For a reaction, a graph of [A] versus time is a straight line. How does the half-life change as the reaction proceeds?
choices: It stays constant, as for every reaction.
It decreases, because a zero-order half-life is proportional to the remaining concentration.
It increases, because the rate slows down.
It is undefined for this reaction.
questions.explanation: A linear [A]-versus-time graph indicates zero order, with \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{2k}\). Each successive half-life is half as long as the one before.

questions.stem: Segment Q rises more slowly than the segment before P, although heat is added at the same rate. What does this indicate?
choices: Liquid water has a greater specific heat capacity than ice.
Liquid water has a smaller specific heat capacity than ice.
Ice has stronger intermolecular forces than liquid water.
Energy is lost to evaporation during segment Q.
questions.explanation: The slope of a heating curve is inversely proportional to the heat capacity. More energy is needed to raise the temperature of liquid water by each degree.

questions.stem: When \(50.0\text{ mL}\) of \(1.00\text{ M}\) HCl and \(50.0\text{ mL}\) of \(1.00\text{ M}\) NaOH are mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter, the temperature rises by \(6.8^\circ\text{C}\). Assuming the solution has a mass of \(100.0\text{ g}\) and a specific heat of \(4.18\text{ J/(g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C)}\), what is \(\Delta H\) of neutralization?
questions.explanation: \(q=(100.0)(4.18)(6.8)=2842\text{ J}\) is absorbed by the solution, so the reaction releases it. Dividing by \(0.0500\text{ mol}\) of water formed gives \(\Delta H\approx -57\text{ kJ/mol}\).

questions.stem: A \(50.0\text{ g}\) metal sample at \(100.0^\circ\text{C}\) is placed in \(100.0\text{ g}\) of water at \(20.0^\circ\text{C}\). The final temperature is \(23.0^\circ\text{C}\). What is the specific heat of the metal? (Water: \(4.18\text{ J/(g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C)}\))
questions.explanation: The water gains \(100.0(4.18)(3.0)=1254\text{ J}\), which the metal loses as it cools by \(77.0^\circ\text{C}\): \(c=\dfrac{1254}{(50.0)(77.0)}\approx 0.33\).

questions.stem: Using average bond enthalpies of \(436\) (H–H), \(242\) (Cl–Cl), and \(431\text{ kJ/mol}\) (H–Cl), what is \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g)\,+\,Cl_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2HCl(g)}\)?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta H=\sum(\text{bonds broken})-\sum(\text{bonds formed})=(436+242)-2(431)=-184\text{ kJ}\). Two H–Cl bonds form.

questions.stem: Given \(\Delta H_f^\circ\) values of \(-74.8\) for \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g)}\), \(-393.5\) for \(\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\), and \(-285.8\text{ kJ/mol}\) for \(\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\), what is \(\Delta H^\circ\) for \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g)\,+\,2O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,CO_{2}(g)\,+\,2H_{2}O(l)}\)?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta H^\circ=[-393.5+2(-285.8)]-[-74.8+0]=-890.3\text{ kJ}\). Elements in their standard states, such as \(\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\), have \(\Delta H_f^\circ=0\).

questions.stem: When \(\mathrm{NH_{4}NO_{3}}\) dissolves in water in a cold pack, the solution becomes cold. Which statement is correct?
choices: The process is endothermic: energy is absorbed from the water, and more energy is needed to separate the ions than is released when they are hydrated.
The process is exothermic, because the solution's temperature changes.
Energy flows from the cold pack into the person's skin.
No bonds or attractions are broken when an ionic solid dissolves.
questions.explanation: Dissolving involves breaking ion–ion attractions and water–water attractions, which absorbs energy, and forming ion–water attractions, which releases energy. Here the net process absorbs energy, lowering the temperature.

questions.stem: A hot iron block is placed in cool water in an insulated container. Which statement describes the system when it reaches thermal equilibrium?
choices: The iron and the water have the same thermal energy.
The iron and the water changed temperature by the same amount.
The iron and the water have the same temperature, and the energy lost by the iron equals the energy gained by the water.
Heat continues to flow from the iron to the water.
questions.explanation: Thermal energy is transferred by collisions until the average kinetic energies, and therefore the temperatures, are equal. Their temperature changes differ because their masses and heat capacities differ.

questions.stem: How much energy is required to melt \(36.0\text{ g}\) of ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\)? (\(\Delta H_{fus}=6.01\text{ kJ/mol}\))
A student's coffee-cup calorimeter loses some heat to the surroundings during an exothermic reaction. How does this affect the calculated magnitude of \(\Delta H\)?
choices: It is too large, because the reaction releases more heat.
It is unaffected, because \(\Delta H\) depends only on the reaction.
It is too large, because the calorimeter absorbs heat.
It is too small, because the measured temperature increase is smaller than it should be.
questions.explanation: The calculation assumes all of the heat released stays in the solution. Heat that escapes is not measured, so the calculated magnitude is too small.

questions.stem: Which reaction has a \(\Delta H^\circ\) equal to the standard enthalpy of formation of liquid water?
questions.explanation: A formation reaction makes exactly one mole of the compound from its elements in their standard states. Hydrogen and oxygen are diatomic gases in their standard states.

questions.stem: Given \(\mathrm{C(s)\,+\,O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,CO_{2}(g)}\), \(\Delta H=-393.5\text{ kJ}\), and \(\mathrm{CO(g)\,+\,1/2O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,CO_{2}(g)}\), \(\Delta H=-283.0\text{ kJ}\), what is \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{C(s)\,+\,1/2O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,CO(g)}\)?
questions.explanation: Keep the first equation and reverse the second: \(-393.5+283.0=-110.5\text{ kJ}\). The \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) cancels, along with half a mole of \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\).

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g)\,+\,3H_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2NH_{3}(g)}\), \(\Delta H=-92\text{ kJ}\). What is \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{4NH_{3}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2N_{2}(g)\,+\,6H_{2}(g)}\)?
questions.explanation: Reversing the reaction changes the sign, and doubling it doubles \(\Delta H\): \(2(+92)=+184\text{ kJ}\).

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{2H_{2}(g)\,+\,O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2H_{2}O(l)}\), \(\Delta H=-572\text{ kJ}\). How much heat is released when \(8.0\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) burns? Use \(2.0\text{ g/mol}\) for \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\).
questions.explanation: \(8.0\text{ g}\) is \(4.0\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\). The \(\Delta H\) given is for \(2\text{ mol}\), so the heat released is \(2(572)=1144\text{ kJ}\).

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the combustion of methane is exothermic?
choices: Breaking the C–H bonds in methane releases energy.
The products have more potential energy than the reactants.
The bonds formed in \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) are, in total, stronger than the bonds broken in \(\mathrm{CH_{4}}\) and \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\).
Oxygen gas stores energy in its double bond, which is released when it breaks.
questions.explanation: Breaking any bond requires energy. More energy is released in forming the strong C=O and O–H bonds than is absorbed in breaking the reactant bonds, so the products are lower in potential energy.

questions.stem: Equal masses of aluminum (\(0.90\text{ J/(g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C)}\)) and iron (\(0.45\text{ J/(g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C)}\)) absorb the same amount of heat. Which statement is correct?
choices: The aluminum's temperature increases twice as much as the iron's.
Both temperatures increase by the same amount.
The aluminum's temperature increases four times as much.
The iron's temperature increases twice as much as the aluminum's.
questions.explanation: \(\Delta T=\dfrac{q}{mc}\). With equal \(q\) and \(m\), halving the specific heat doubles the temperature change.

questions.stem: Which statement about an exothermic process at constant pressure is correct?
choices: \(q\) for the system is positive, and the surroundings cool down.
\(\Delta H\) is positive, because energy is released.
\(q\) for the system is negative, \(\Delta H\) is negative, and the surroundings warm up.
The system gains energy from the surroundings.
questions.explanation: In an exothermic process the system transfers energy to the surroundings, so the system's \(q\) and \(\Delta H\) are negative.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of a substance much greater than its enthalpy of fusion?
choices: Vaporization breaks covalent bonds, while melting does not.
Vaporization separates molecules almost completely, overcoming nearly all intermolecular attractions, while melting overcomes only some of them.
Vaporization occurs at a higher temperature, which requires more energy.
Melting releases energy, while vaporization absorbs it.
questions.explanation: In a liquid, molecules are still close together and attract one another. Converting the liquid to a gas pulls them far apart, which requires much more energy.

questions.stem: How much heat is needed to warm \(250\text{ g}\) of water from \(20.0^\circ\text{C}\) to \(80.0^\circ\text{C}\)? (\(c=4.18\text{ J/(g}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C)}\))
questions.explanation: \(q=mc\Delta T=250(4.18)(60.0)=62{,}700\text{ J}=62.7\text{ kJ}\). Using the final temperature instead of the change gives \(83.6\text{ kJ}\).

questions.stem: On an energy diagram for an endothermic reaction, how are the reactants and products positioned?
choices: The products are lower in energy than the reactants, and \(\Delta H\) is positive.
The products and reactants are at the same energy.
The products are higher in energy than the reactants, and \(\Delta H\) is positive.
The transition state is lower than the products.
questions.explanation: An endothermic reaction absorbs energy, so the products store more potential energy. The transition state is always at the top of the energy barrier.

questions.stem: Given \(\mathrm{S(s)\,+\,O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,SO_{2}(g)}\), \(\Delta H=-297\text{ kJ}\), and \(\mathrm{2SO_{3}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2SO_{2}(g)\,+\,O_{2}(g)}\), \(\Delta H=+198\text{ kJ}\), what is \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{S(s)\,+\,3/2O_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,SO_{3}(g)}\)?
questions.explanation: Keep the first equation, and reverse and halve the second: \(-297+\tfrac{1}{2}(-198)=-297-99=-396\text{ kJ}\).

questions.stem: What is the equilibrium constant expression \(K_p\) for \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)\,\rightleftharpoons\,CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)}\)?
questions.explanation: Pure solids are omitted from equilibrium expressions because their concentrations do not change. Only the partial pressure of the gas appears.

questions.stem: For a reaction, \(K=4.0\times 10^{-3}\). In a mixture, \(Q=2.0\times 10^{-2}\). Which statement is correct?
choices: The reaction proceeds toward products until \(Q=K\).
The reaction proceeds toward reactants until \(Q=K\).
questions.explanation: Since \(Q>K\), the ratio of products to reactants is too large. The reverse reaction is faster until the ratio decreases to \(K\).

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g)\,+\,I_{2}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2HI(g)}\), \(K_c=49\). If \(1.0\text{ mol}\) each of \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) are placed in a \(1.0\text{ L}\) container, what is [HI] at equilibrium?
questions.explanation: With \(x\) mol/L reacting, \(\dfrac{(2x)^2}{(1.0-x)^2}=49\), so \(\dfrac{2x}{1.0-x}=7\) and \(x=\tfrac{7}{9}\approx 0.78\). Then \([\mathrm{HI}]=2x\approx 1.56\text{ M}\).

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g)\,+\,3H_{2}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2NH_{3}(g)}\), the equilibrium constant is \(K\). What is the equilibrium constant for \(\mathrm{4NH_{3}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2N_{2}(g)\,+\,6H_{2}(g)}\)?
questions.explanation: Reversing a reaction inverts \(K\), and multiplying the coefficients by 2 squares it.

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2NO_{2}(g)}\) at \(400\text{ K}\), \(K_c=1.0\). What is \(K_p\)? Use \(R=0.0821\text{ L}\cdot\text{atm/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}\).
Argon gas is added to an equilibrium mixture of \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\), and \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) in a rigid container. How does the equilibrium respond?
choices: It shifts toward \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\), because the total pressure increases.
It does not shift, because the partial pressures of the reacting gases do not change.
questions.explanation: In a fixed volume, adding an inert gas leaves the concentrations of the reacting species unchanged, so \(Q\) still equals \(K\).

questions.stem: The volume of a container holding \(\mathrm{2SO_{2}(g)\,+\,O_{2}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2SO_{3}(g)}\) at equilibrium is halved at constant temperature. What happens?
choices: Nothing, because the temperature is constant.
The equilibrium shifts toward \(\mathrm{SO_{3}}\), the side with fewer moles of gas.
questions.explanation: Halving the volume doubles all partial pressures, making \(Q<K\) because the product side has fewer moles of gas. The system shifts forward to restore \(Q=K\); \(K\) itself does not change.

questions.stem: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, the temperature is raised. How do \(K\) and the amounts of products change?
choices: \(K\) increases, and the amounts of products increase.
\(K\) stays the same, but the amounts of products decrease.
\(K\) decreases, and the amounts of products decrease.
\(K\) decreases, but the amounts of products increase.
questions.explanation: Heat behaves like a product of an exothermic reaction. Raising the temperature favors the reverse, endothermic direction, which lowers \(K\). Temperature is the only change that alters \(K\).

figure.alt: Concentrations over time for the reaction N2O4 ⇌ 2 NO2 in a sealed container. N2O4 starts at 0.100 M and falls to a constant 0.060 M; NO2 starts at 0 and rises to a constant 0.080 M by about 3 minutes. At 5 minutes, NO2 suddenly increases to 0.120 M. Afterward NO2 decreases to about 0.090 M while N2O4 increases to about 0.075 M, and both become constant again

questions.stem: What change was made to the system at 5 minutes, and how did the system respond?
choices: \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\) was added, and the system shifted toward \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\).
\(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) was added, and the system shifted toward \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\).
The temperature was raised, and the system shifted toward \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\).
A catalyst was added, and the system shifted toward \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\).
questions.explanation: Only \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) jumps suddenly at 5 minutes. Afterward \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\) decreases and \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}}\) increases as the reverse reaction consumes the added \(\mathrm{NO_{2}}\). A catalyst would not shift the equilibrium.

figure.alt: Concentrations over time for the reaction N2O4 ⇌ 2 NO2 in a sealed container. N2O4 starts at 0.100 M and falls to a constant 0.060 M; NO2 starts at 0 and rises to a constant 0.080 M by about 3 minutes. At 5 minutes, NO2 suddenly increases to 0.120 M. Afterward NO2 decreases to about 0.090 M while N2O4 increases to about 0.075 M, and both become constant again

questions.stem: Based on the graph, what is \(K_c\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}O_{4}\,\rightleftharpoons\,2NO_{2}}\) under these conditions?
questions.explanation: Before 5 minutes, \(K_c=\dfrac{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2O_4}]}=\dfrac{(0.080)^2}{0.060}\approx 0.11\). The new equilibrium after 5 minutes gives the same value, \(\tfrac{(0.090)^2}{0.075}\).

questions.stem: The molar solubility of \(\mathrm{PbI_{2}}\) is \(1.5\times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\). What is its \(K_{sp}\)?
questions.explanation: Dissolving \(s\) mol/L gives \([\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}]=s\) and \([\mathrm{I^-}]=2s\), so \(K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3=4(1.5\times 10^{-3})^3\approx 1.4\times 10^{-8}\).

questions.stem: Which compound in the table has the greatest molar solubility in pure water?
questions.explanation: \(K_{sp}\) values can be compared directly only for salts with the same ion ratio. For \(\mathrm{CaF_{2}}\), \(s=\sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}\approx 2.1\times 10^{-4}\text{ M}\), greater than for the others; AgCl, despite the largest \(K_{sp}\), has \(s\approx 1.3\times 10^{-5}\text{ M}\).

questions.stem: What is the molar solubility of AgCl in \(0.10\text{ M}\) NaCl?
questions.explanation: With \([\mathrm{Cl^-}]\approx 0.10\text{ M}\), \(s=\dfrac{1.8\times 10^{-10}}{0.10}=1.8\times 10^{-9}\text{ M}\), far less than in pure water.

figure.alt: Table of solubility-product constants at 25 °C: AgCl, 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰; Ag2CrO4, 1.1 × 10⁻¹²; CaF2, 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹; Mg(OH)2, 5.6 × 10⁻¹²

questions.stem: Which compound in the table becomes much more soluble when the solution is acidified?
choices: None, because pH does not affect solubility
questions.explanation: Added \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), removing a product of the dissolution and shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving. Chloride is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so AgCl is unaffected.

questions.stem: Equal volumes of \(2.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{AgNO_{3}}\) and \(2.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ M}\) NaCl are mixed. Does a precipitate form? (\(K_{sp}\) of AgCl \(=1.8\times 10^{-10}\))
choices: Yes, because \(Q=1.0\times 10^{-8}\), which is greater than \(K_{sp}\)
Yes, because \(Q=4.0\times 10^{-8}\), which is greater than \(K_{sp}\)
It cannot be determined without the actual volumes
questions.explanation: Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration to \(1.0\times 10^{-4}\text{ M}\), so \(Q=(1.0\times 10^{-4})^2=1.0\times 10^{-8}\), which exceeds \(K_{sp}\). Using the undiluted concentrations gives the incorrect \(4.0\times 10^{-8}\).

questions.stem: For a reaction at \(25^\circ\text{C}\), \(K=3\times 10^{-15}\). Which statement is correct?
choices: At equilibrium, the mixture consists mostly of products.
At equilibrium, the mixture consists mostly of reactants.
questions.explanation: A very small \(K\) means the ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium is tiny. \(K\) says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

questions.stem: A small amount of radioactive \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) is added to a saturated solution in contact with solid \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\). Later, radioactivity is found in the solid. What does this show?
choices: Dissolving and crystallizing continue at equal rates at equilibrium.
Radioactive iodine is less soluble than ordinary iodine.
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic: molecules continuously leave and rejoin the solid, so labeled molecules end up in the solid even though the amounts do not change.

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{A(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2B(g)}\), \(K_c=4.0\times 10^{-4}\). If \(0.10\text{ M}\) A is placed in a container, what is [B] at equilibrium?
questions.explanation: With \(x\) reacting, \(\dfrac{(2x)^2}{0.10-x}\approx\dfrac{4x^2}{0.10}=4.0\times 10^{-4}\), so \(x\approx 3.2\times 10^{-3}\). Then \([\mathrm{B}]=2x\approx 6.3\times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\).

questions.stem: More solid \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) is added to the equilibrium \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)\,\rightleftharpoons\,CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)}\) in a closed container. What happens to the pressure of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\)?
questions.explanation: Pure solids do not appear in the equilibrium expression, so adding solid does not change \(Q\). The \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) pressure remains equal to \(K_p\).

questions.stem: A catalyst is added to a reaction mixture at equilibrium. What happens?
choices: Nothing changes, because the catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally.
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both directions by the same amount, so it does not change the equilibrium position or \(K\). It only helps a system reach equilibrium faster.

questions.stem: A closed container at equilibrium for \(\mathrm{X_{2}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,2X(g)}\) holds 4 \(\mathrm{X_{2}}\) molecules and 4 X atoms in a volume where each particle represents \(0.10\text{ M}\). What is \(K_c\)?
questions.explanation: \([\mathrm{X}]=0.40\text{ M}\) and \([\mathrm{X_2}]=0.40\text{ M}\), so \(K_c=\dfrac{(0.40)^2}{0.40}=0.40\). The particle counts alone, without concentration, would give \(\tfrac{16}{4}=4\).

questions.stem: At equilibrium for \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}(g)\,\rightleftharpoons\,PCl_{3}(g)\,+\,Cl_{2}(g)}\), the partial pressures are \(0.50\text{ atm}\) for \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}}\) and \(0.20\text{ atm}\) each for \(\mathrm{PCl_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\). What is \(K_p\)?
questions.explanation: \(K_p=\dfrac{P_{\mathrm{PCl_3}}P_{\mathrm{Cl_2}}}{P_{\mathrm{PCl_5}}}=\dfrac{(0.20)(0.20)}{0.50}=0.080\). Adding the product pressures instead of multiplying them gives \(0.80\).

questions.stem: What is the pH of \(0.0050\text{ M}\) HCl?
questions.explanation: HCl ionizes completely, so \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]=0.0050\text{ M}\) and \(\text{pH}=-\log(0.0050)=2.30\).

questions.stem: What is the pH of \(0.020\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_{2}}\)?
questions.explanation: Each formula unit releases two \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), so \([\mathrm{OH^-}]=0.040\text{ M}\), \(\text{pOH}=1.40\), and \(\text{pH}=12.60\). Forgetting the 2 gives \(12.30\).

questions.stem: What is the pH of \(0.10\text{ M}\) acetic acid (\(K_a=1.8\times 10^{-5}\))?
questions.explanation: \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\approx\sqrt{K_aC}=\sqrt{1.8\times 10^{-6}}=1.34\times 10^{-3}\text{ M}\), so \(\text{pH}=2.87\). A pH of \(1.00\) would apply to a strong acid.

questions.stem: How does the percent ionization of a weak acid change when its solution is diluted?
choices: It decreases, because there is less acid.
It increases, because the equilibrium shifts toward the side with more dissolved particles.
It does not change, because \(K_a\) is constant.
questions.explanation: Diluting lowers every concentration, making \(Q<K_a\). The acid ionizes further, so a larger fraction is ionized even though \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\) decreases.

questions.stem: The \(K_a\) of acetic acid is \(1.8\times 10^{-5}\). What is \(K_b\) for the acetate ion?
questions.explanation: For a conjugate acid–base pair, \(K_aK_b=K_w=1.0\times 10^{-14}\), so \(K_b=\dfrac{1.0\times 10^{-14}}{1.8\times 10^{-5}}=5.6\times 10^{-10}\).

figure.alt: Titration curve for 20.0 mL of a 0.100 M weak monoprotic acid titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. The pH starts near 2.9, rises gradually through a buffer region, and passes point J at 10.0 mL, where the pH is about 4.7. It rises steeply near point K at 20.0 mL, the equivalence point, where the pH is about 8.7, and levels off near 12.5

questions.stem: Based on the titration curve, what is \(K_a\) of the acid?
questions.explanation: At point J, the half-equivalence point, half of the acid has been converted to its conjugate base, so \([\mathrm{HA}]=[\mathrm{A^-}]\) and \(\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a\approx 4.7\). Then \(K_a=10^{-4.7}\approx 2\times 10^{-5}\).

The pH starts near 2.9, rises gradually through a buffer region, and passes point J at 10.0 mL, where the pH is about 4.7. It rises steeply near point K at 20.0 mL, the equivalence point, where the pH is about 8.7, and levels off near 12.5

questions.stem: Why is the pH at point K greater than 7?
choices: At the equivalence point the solution contains the conjugate base of a weak acid, which reacts with water to produce \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\).
Some of the weak acid remains un-ionized.
questions.explanation: All of the HA has become \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\), which is a weak base: \(\mathrm{A^{-}\,+\,H_{2}O\,\rightleftharpoons\,HA\,+\,OH^{-}}\). \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) has no effect on pH.

The pH starts near 2.9, rises gradually through a buffer region, and passes point J at 10.0 mL, where the pH is about 4.7. It rises steeply near point K at 20.0 mL, the equivalence point, where the pH is about 8.7, and levels off near 12.5

questions.stem: Which indicator is most suitable for the titration shown?
choices: Methyl orange, which changes color between pH 3.1 and 4.4
Methyl red, which changes color between pH 4.4 and 6.2
Phenolphthalein, which changes color between pH 8.2 and 10
Any indicator, because all change color at pH 7
questions.explanation: An indicator should change color within the steep rise around the equivalence point, which is centered near pH 8.7. Methyl orange would change color early, in the buffer region.

The pH starts near 2.9, rises gradually through a buffer region, and passes point J at 10.0 mL, where the pH is about 4.7. It rises steeply near point K at 20.0 mL, the equivalence point, where the pH is about 8.7, and levels off near 12.5

questions.stem: After \(30.0\text{ mL}\) of NaOH have been added in the titration shown, which species is present in the greatest amount, other than water and \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\)?
questions.explanation: Of the \(3.0\text{ mmol}\) of \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) added, \(2.0\text{ mmol}\) converted all of the HA to \(2.0\text{ mmol}\) of \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\), leaving \(1.0\text{ mmol}\) of excess \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a buffer that is \(0.20\text{ M}\) acetic acid and \(0.10\text{ M}\) sodium acetate (\(\text{p}K_a=4.74\))?
questions.explanation: \(\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a+\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}=4.74+\log 0.5=4.44\). With more acid than base, the pH is below the \(\text{p}K_a\).

questions.stem: Buffer 1 is \(0.50\text{ M}\) HA and \(0.50\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\); buffer 2 is \(0.050\text{ M}\) HA and \(0.050\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\). Which statement is correct?
choices: They have the same pH, but buffer 1 can neutralize more added acid or base.
Buffer 2 has a greater capacity because it is more dilute.
They have the same capacity because the ratios are equal.
questions.explanation: pH depends on the ratio \(\tfrac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}\), which is 1 for both. Capacity depends on the amounts of HA and \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\) available to react, which is ten times greater in buffer 1.

questions.stem: A small amount of HCl is added to an acetic acid–acetate buffer. Which reaction occurs?
questions.explanation: The base component of the buffer consumes the added strong acid, converting it to the weak acid. The ratio of base to acid changes only slightly, so the pH barely changes.

figure.alt: Table of acids with Ka and pKa: formic acid, 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, 3.74; acetic acid, 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, 4.74; dihydrogen phosphate, 6.2 × 10⁻⁸, 7.21; ammonium, 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, 9.25

questions.stem: A student needs a buffer with a pH of about \(9.2\). Which acid–conjugate base pair from the table is the best choice?
questions.explanation: A buffer works best when \(\text{pH}\approx\text{p}K_a\), so that both components are present in similar amounts. The \(\text{p}K_a\) of ammonium is \(9.25\).

questions.stem: A solution of formic acid is adjusted to pH \(7.0\). Which form predominates?
questions.explanation: When the pH is above the \(\text{p}K_a\), here \(3.74\), the deprotonated form predominates. At pH 7, the ratio of formate to formic acid is \(10^{3.26}\), about 1800 to 1.

questions.stem: In a solution of acetic acid at pH \(5.74\), what is the ratio \(\dfrac{[\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}]}{[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]}\)?
questions.explanation: \(\text{pH}-\text{p}K_a=5.74-4.74=1.00\), so \(\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}=1.00\) and the ratio is \(10\).

Two rises appear: the first equivalence point at 20.0 mL (point X, pH about 5) and the second at 40.0 mL (pH about 10). Point W at 10.0 mL has a pH of about 3.0, and point Y at 30.0 mL has a pH of about 7.0

questions.stem: In the titration of the diprotic acid shown, what is the main form of the acid at point X?
questions.explanation: Point X, at \(20.0\text{ mL}\), is the first equivalence point: exactly one proton has been removed from each \(\mathrm{H_{2}A}\).

Two rises appear: the first equivalence point at 20.0 mL (point X, pH about 5) and the second at 40.0 mL (pH about 10). Point W at 10.0 mL has a pH of about 3.0, and point Y at 30.0 mL has a pH of about 7.0

questions.stem: Based on the titration curve, what are the two \(\text{p}K_a\) values of the acid?
questions.explanation: Point W is halfway to the first equivalence point, where \([\mathrm{H_2A}]=[\mathrm{HA^-}]\) and \(\text{pH}=\text{p}K_{a1}\). Point Y is halfway between the two equivalence points, where \([\mathrm{HA^-}]=[\mathrm{A^{2-}}]\) and \(\text{pH}=\text{p}K_{a2}\).

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why HF is a weak acid while HCl is a strong acid?
choices: Fluorine is less electronegative than chlorine.
HF molecules are larger than HCl molecules.
HF does not dissolve in water.
The H–F bond is much stronger than the H–Cl bond, so HF ionizes less in water.
questions.explanation: Bond strength matters more than electronegativity in this case. The small fluorine atom forms a short, strong bond with hydrogen, so HF only partly ionizes.

questions.stem: Which salt forms an acidic solution when dissolved in water?
questions.explanation: \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) is a weak acid that donates protons to water, while \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is a negligible base. Sodium acetate is basic, and NaCl and \(\mathrm{KNO_{3}}\) are neutral.

questions.stem: At \(50^\circ\text{C}\), \(K_w=5.5\times 10^{-14}\). What is true of pure water at this temperature?
choices: It is acidic, because its pH is less than 7.
Its pH is less than 7, but it is still neutral because \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]=[\mathrm{OH^-}]\).
questions.explanation: \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]=\sqrt{5.5\times 10^{-14}}\approx 2.3\times 10^{-7}\), so the pH is about \(6.6\). Neutrality means equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide, not a pH of 7.

questions.stem: \(50.0\text{ mL}\) of \(0.10\text{ M}\) HCl is mixed with \(50.0\text{ mL}\) of \(0.10\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\). What is the pH of the resulting solution? (\(K_a\) of \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) \(=5.6\times 10^{-10}\))
questions.explanation: The acid and base neutralize exactly, forming \(0.050\text{ M}\) \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\). Then \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]=\sqrt{(5.6\times 10^{-10})(0.050)}\approx 5.3\times 10^{-6}\), so the pH is about \(5.3\).

questions.stem: A \(0.050\text{ M}\) solution of a weak acid HA has a pH of \(3.00\). What is \(K_a\) of HA?
Which reaction has a negative \(\Delta S^\circ\)?
questions.explanation: Three moles of gas become two, decreasing the number of ways energy and matter can be dispersed. The other reactions produce gas.

questions.stem: A reaction has \(\Delta H>0\) and \(\Delta S>0\). Under which conditions is it thermodynamically favored?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S\). The positive \(\Delta H\) works against the reaction, so it is favored only when \(T\Delta S\) is large enough to make \(\Delta G\) negative.

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s)\,\longrightarrow\,CaO(s)\,+\,CO_{2}(g)}\), \(\Delta H^\circ=+178\text{ kJ/mol}\) and \(\Delta S^\circ=+161\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}\). Above about what temperature is the reaction thermodynamically favored?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta G=0\) when \(T=\dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}=\dfrac{178{,}000}{161}\approx 1100\text{ K}\). Forgetting to convert kJ to J gives \(1.1\text{ K}\).

questions.stem: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g)\,+\,3H_{2}(g)\,\longrightarrow\,2NH_{3}(g)}\), \(\Delta H^\circ=-92.2\text{ kJ}\) and \(\Delta S^\circ=-198.7\text{ J/K}\). What is \(\Delta G^\circ\) at \(298\text{ K}\)?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta G^\circ=-92.2-298(-0.1987)=-92.2+59.2=-33.0\text{ kJ}\). Adding \(T\Delta S\) instead of subtracting gives \(-151.4\).

questions.stem: For a reaction at \(298\text{ K}\), \(\Delta G^\circ=-33.0\text{ kJ/mol}\). Approximately what is \(K\)?
questions.explanation: \(K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}=e^{33{,}000/(8.314\times 298)}=e^{13.3}\approx 6\times 10^{5}\). A negative \(\Delta G^\circ\) always corresponds to \(K>1\).

questions.stem: The conversion of diamond to graphite has \(\Delta G^\circ<0\), yet diamonds last for millions of years. Which best explains this?
choices: \(\Delta G^\circ\) is positive at room temperature.
The reaction has a very large activation energy, so it is extremely slow at room temperature.
Diamond is in equilibrium with graphite.
The reaction requires a catalyst to be thermodynamically favored.
questions.explanation: A negative \(\Delta G\) shows only that products are favored, not how fast they form. The process is under kinetic control.

questions.stem: A reaction with \(\Delta G^\circ=+20\text{ kJ}\) is coupled with the hydrolysis of ATP, \(\Delta G^\circ=-30\text{ kJ}\). Which statement is correct?
choices: The combined process has \(\Delta G^\circ=+50\text{ kJ}\).
The combined process has \(\Delta G^\circ=-10\text{ kJ}\) and is thermodynamically favored.
Coupling makes the first reaction faster but not favored.
Coupling is impossible because the reactions have opposite signs.
questions.explanation: Free energies of reactions that share an intermediate add. Living cells drive unfavorable reactions by coupling them to favorable ones such as ATP hydrolysis.
