questions.stem: In the cell shown, which electrode is the anode, and in which direction do electrons flow through the wire?
choices: The copper electrode; from copper to zinc
The zinc electrode; from copper to zinc
The copper electrode; from zinc to copper
The zinc electrode; from zinc to copper
questions.explanation: Zinc has the more negative reduction potential, so it is oxidized at the anode: \(\mathrm{Zn\,\longrightarrow\,Zn^{2+}\,+\,2e^{-}}\). Electrons travel through the wire to the copper cathode, where \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is reduced.

questions.stem: As the cell shown operates, which ions move through the salt bridge, and in which directions?
choices: \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\) toward the zinc compartment and \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\) toward the copper compartment
\(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\) toward the copper compartment and \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\) toward the zinc compartment
\(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) through the salt bridge to the copper compartment
Electrons through the salt bridge to the zinc compartment
questions.explanation: The anode compartment gains \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), so anions flow in to keep it neutral; the cathode compartment loses \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), so cations flow in. Electrons never travel through the solution.

questions.stem: Using the table of reduction potentials, what is \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) for the cell shown?
questions.explanation: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}-E^\circ_{\text{anode}}=0.34-(-0.76)=1.10\text{ V}\). A positive cell potential means the reaction is thermodynamically favored.

questions.stem: What is \(\Delta G^\circ\) for the reaction in the cell shown, \(\mathrm{Zn(s)\,+\,Cu^{2+}(aq)\,\longrightarrow\,Zn^{2+}(aq)\,+\,Cu(s)}\), with \(E^\circ=1.10\text{ V}\)? (\(F=96{,}485\text{ C/mol}\))
questions.explanation: \(\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ=-(2)(96{,}485)(1.10)=-212{,}000\text{ J}\). Two moles of electrons transfer per mole of reaction.

questions.stem: Which species in the table is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.explanation: The metal whose ion has the most negative reduction potential is most easily oxidized, so it most readily gives electrons to other species. \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) is the strongest oxidizing agent.

questions.stem: What is the standard cell potential of a galvanic cell made from aluminum and silver half-cells?
questions.explanation: \(E^\circ=0.80-(-1.66)=2.46\text{ V}\). The reduction potential is an intensive property, so it is not multiplied by the coefficients needed to balance electrons.

questions.stem: In the zinc–copper cell, the concentration of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is increased while \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) stays at \(1.0\text{ M}\). How does the cell potential change?
choices: It increases, because \(Q\) decreases and the reaction is driven further toward products.
It decreases, because more copper ions must be reduced.
questions.explanation: \(Q=\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]}\) decreases. As \(Q\) falls below 1, the cell potential rises above \(E^\circ\).

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has run until its voltage is zero. Which statement is true?
choices: All of the reactants have been used up.
The cell reaction has reached equilibrium, so \(Q=K\) and \(\Delta G=0\).
questions.explanation: A dead battery has no remaining driving force: \(\Delta G=-nFE=0\). The standard potential \(E^\circ\) is a fixed property of the reaction.

questions.stem: How long must a current of \(2.00\text{ A}\) flow to deposit \(1.00\text{ g}\) of copper from a \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) solution? (\(F=96{,}485\text{ C/mol}\))
questions.explanation: \(\tfrac{1.00}{63.55}=0.0157\text{ mol}\) Cu requires \(0.0315\text{ mol}\) of electrons, or \(3040\text{ C}\). At \(2.00\text{ C/s}\), this takes about \(1520\text{ s}\).

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of molten NaCl, what forms at the cathode?
questions.explanation: Reduction occurs at the cathode: \(\mathrm{Na^{+}\,+\,e^{-}\,\longrightarrow\,Na}\). Chloride is oxidized to \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) at the anode. In molten salt there is no water to be reduced.

questions.stem: Which sample has the greatest standard molar entropy?
questions.explanation: Gases have far more freedom of motion and positional possibilities than liquids and solids. Among phases of the same substance, \(S_{\text{gas}}>S_{\text{liquid}}>S_{\text{solid}}\).

questions.stem: A reaction has a positive \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\). Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ\) and \(\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K\). A positive \(E^\circ\) gives a negative \(\Delta G^\circ\), which corresponds to \(K>1\).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts galvanic and electrolytic cells?
choices: Both use favored reactions to produce electricity.
In an electrolytic cell, oxidation occurs at the cathode.
A galvanic cell has a negative cell potential.
A galvanic cell uses a thermodynamically favored reaction to produce electricity, while an electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive an unfavored reaction.
questions.explanation: In both kinds of cells, oxidation occurs at the anode. An electrolytic cell needs an external power source because \(\Delta G>0\) for its reaction.

questions.stem: When a gas dissolves in water, \(\Delta S\) for the process is typically negative. Which best explains this?
choices: Gas molecules lose much of their freedom of motion when they become surrounded by water molecules.
The water molecules gain freedom of motion.
The gas reacts to form a solid.
questions.explanation: Dispersing gas molecules into a much smaller volume within the liquid restricts their motion. That is why gases are less soluble at higher temperatures, where the \(-T\Delta S\) term matters more.

questions.stem: For a reaction at \(400\text{ K}\), \(\Delta H^\circ=-50\text{ kJ}\) and \(\Delta S^\circ=-100\text{ J/K}\). What is \(\Delta G^\circ\), and is the reaction favored?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta G^\circ=-50-400(-0.100)=-50+40=-10\text{ kJ}\). Above \(500\text{ K}\), the entropy term would make \(\Delta G^\circ\) positive.
